Empirical Research Plan – Connecticut Elementary-School Class Size  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
I will implement a multi-cutoff fuzzy regression-discontinuity / 2-stage-least-squares design.  
• Running variable: grade-level enrollment in a school-year.  
• Cut-offs: each district’s binding maximum (and, symmetrically, minimum) class-size rule.  
• First stage: when enrollment crosses a cutoff the school is forced to add (or drop) an entire classroom, producing a discrete jump in average class size (≈ 4–6 pupils).  
Because the enrollment shocks are driven by idiosyncratic birth-cohort fluctuations that districts cannot legally control ex post, this sharp, rule-based change is plausibly as-good-as randomized. The resulting design is equivalent to Angrist & Lavy (1999) “Maimonides Rule,” i.e. a fuzzy RDD estimated as IV, with plenty of distance from policy endogeneity or parental choice (Connecticut elementary schools rarely allow within-district choice).  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
  T = actual average class size in grade g of school s during year t.  
Instrument (Z)  
  Predicted class size = Enroll_sgt / ⎡Enroll_sgt / MaxRule_d⎤, where MaxRule_d is the district’s ceiling.  
Control vs. treated comparison  
  Units with enrollment just below a cutoff (k·MaxRule_d) are the control; units just above are “treated” with a smaller class size (because one more classroom is added).  
Treatment timing  
  “Event” occurs contemporaneously: the cohort that triggers an additional classroom enjoys the smaller class size in that same academic year.  
Running variable & cutoffs  
  RV = Enroll_sgt – k·MaxRule_d (centered at each integer multiple k). The same logic applies symmetrically at the minimum rule, where losing a classroom raises average class size.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1 Continuity of potential outcomes in enrollment at the cutoffs.  
  Plausible: birth-cohort size in small CT towns is driven by fertility timing, not by educational quality.  
A2 No precise manipulation of enrollment around the thresholds.  
  Plausible: K-3 parents cannot forecast next year’s fourth-grade cutoff; schools must accept all resident children.  
A3 First-stage relevance: crossing a cutoff moves class size materially.  
  Supported by modal caps 25/15 and observed SD = 5.5 pupils. This is testable.  
A4 Exclusion restriction: enrollment affects achievement only through the induced change in class size (no direct peer-cohort or resource effects).  
  Plausible in elementary grades where resources are allocated per classroom; we can partially test by showing no jump in per-pupil spending or teacher quality at thresholds.  
A5 Monotonicity: adding a classroom never increases a child’s class size.  
  Guaranteed by the mechanical rule.  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
T1 Non-class-size mechanisms of enrollment shocks (peer quality, crowding).  
  • Control for cohort-size polynomial in the second stage.  
  • Test for jumps in observable peer demographics at cutoffs.  
T2 Sorting or redistricting that lets parents select schools when class size becomes known.  
  • McCrary test for bunching of enrollment just below the cutoff.  
  • Exclude districts with open enrollment policies; show robustness to including residential mobility controls from Census.  
T3 Measurement error in class size or cap parameters.  
  • Use superintendent survey to verify cap stability.  
  • Instrumented design already attenuates measurement error bias; cluster SEs at the school level.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE + IV
library(rddensity)    # McCrary test
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
sch <- fread("ct_school_panel.csv")         # enrollment & class size
rules <- fread("ct_classsize_rules.csv")    # min / max caps
tests <- fread("ct_test_scores.csv")        # normalized scores

# merge
dat <- merge(sch, rules, by = "district_id")
dat <- merge(dat, tests, by = c("school_id","grade","cohort"))

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
dat[, k := round(enrollment / max_cap)]                      # integer multiple
dat[, cutoff := k * max_cap]                                 # nearest threshold
dat[, running := enrollment - cutoff]                        # centered RV
dat[, predicted_cs := enrollment / ceiling(enrollment / max_cap)]

# demographic interaction for heterogeneity
dat[, low_income := (pct_free_lunch > median(pct_free_lunch, na.rm = TRUE))]
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main fuzzy-RDD / 2SLS
#  Bandwidth: +/- 20 pupils around each cutoff
bw <- 20
sample <- dat[abs(running) <= bw]

est <- feols(score ~ 1 |                                                # second stage
             0 |                                                        # no controls beyond FE
             actual_cs ~ predicted_cs,                                  # 2SLS
             data = sample,
             fixef = ~ school_id + grade + cohort)                      # saturated FEs

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: alternative polynomial in RV & placebo test
robust <- feols(score ~ poly(running, 2) | school_id + grade + cohort | 
                actual_cs ~ predicted_cs,
                data = sample)

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Density test for sorting
dens <- rddensity(x = dat$running, c = 0)
summary(dens)
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory and prior evidence (STAR, Angrist-Lavy) suggest a negative effect: –0.02 to –0.04 SD in test score per additional pupil. I expect larger effects (in absolute value) in predominantly low-income or minority schools because class size may substitute for home inputs.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (fuzzy RDD / IV version)  
C1 Continuity of potential outcomes at cutoff ………………… 0.8  
C2 No sorting around cutoff (McCrary) …………………………… 0.9  
C3 Strong first stage (F-stat > 10) ………………………………… 1.0  
C4 Exclusion / no other discontinuities ………………………… 0.7  
C5 Correct functional form & bandwidth choice ……………… 0.8  

Overall: The design is likely credible but hinges on demonstrating no discontinuous peer-quality or funding changes and verifying bandwidth robustness.
